title: ‘Unstable counterpart’: Danish lawmaker worries President Donald Trump doesn’t understand the Greenland security agreement his administration just negotiated
content:
A Danish lawmaker has questioned whether President Donald Trump fully understands the Greenland security agreement negotiated by his administration, warning that reaching an agreement with an unpredictable White House carries significant risks.

Mads Fuglede of the Denmark Democrats raised the concerns during a debate in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, on November 12, 2026. He said Copenhagen had secured an agreement with an “unstable counterpart” despite months of extraordinary pressure from Washington.

Fuglede nevertheless defended the deal, describing it as a diplomatic achievement and arguing that Europe cannot afford to abandon its security relationship with the United States.

What Fuglede told Parliament

“You naturally run a risk when you enter into an agreement with a party who, not very long after the agreement, also expresses on social media and elsewhere that he probably hasn’t entirely understood what kind of agreement he has entered into,” Fuglede told fellow lawmakers.

He said the Trump administration had become an exceptionally difficult partner with which to negotiate binding agreements.

Despite his reservations, Fuglede confirmed his party’s full support for the agreement. He said Denmark and Greenland had negotiated successfully with a considerably more powerful country and stressed the importance of maintaining transatlantic security ties.

“We cannot do without them in our European security structure,” he said.

What the Greenland agreement includes

The parliamentary debate focused on a security agreement that would allow the United States to expand its military presence in Greenland.

The agreement requires approval from both the Folketing and Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, before taking effect. It reaffirms Danish sovereignty over Greenland and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination.

Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the agreement in New York on September 22, 2026.

Building on a 1951 defense treaty, the deal permits expanded American operations at Pituffik Space Base and provides for additional defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, subject to further arrangements. It also strengthens NATO cooperation in the Arctic and establishes a framework for additional U.S. military facilities.

The agreement includes provisions concerning Greenlandic businesses and environmental protections.

Danish lawmakers weigh the risks

Although several lawmakers criticized Trump’s approach to Greenland, representatives from across Denmark’s political spectrum welcomed the agreement.

Sjúrður Skaale, who represents the Faroe Islands, recalled attending meetings at Denmark’s foreign ministry and prime minister’s office during Trump’s renewed push to acquire Greenland.

The message conveyed during those discussions, he said, could be summarized in three words: “He means it.”

Skaale said Denmark sought international support, including efforts to persuade other countries to send troops to Greenland. He described the negotiations as exceptionally difficult because Denmark and Greenland were economically, politically and militarily weaker than the United States.

Nevertheless, he called the outcome a diplomatic achievement.

“I think the agreement is truly a masterpiece,” he said.

Skaale also questioned whether Trump’s commitments could be trusted. He referred to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney‘s comparison of American agreements to signatures written in pencil that can later be erased.

“We can only hope that it does not end up like a certain agreement that the president made with Canada, which did not remain valid for very long,” Skaale said.

Karsten Hønge of the Green Left highlighted the anxiety experienced by Greenlandic families during the dispute. He said children had asked their parents whether American forces would occupy the island and where their families would have to move.

“In Denmark, we were nervous and frustrated. But in Greenland, ordinary people were afraid,” he said.

Helle Bonnesen, a Conservative lawmaker, said Greenlanders had faced “completely inhuman pressure.”

Thomas Rohden of the Social Liberal Party described the dispute as potentially Denmark’s biggest foreign-policy crisis since World War II.

“We have stood firm that Greenland is not for sale,” he said, adding that Greenlanders must decide their own future.

Trine Pertou Mach of the Red-Green Alliance accused Washington of threatening to seize Greenland by force and showing unprecedented disregard for international law. Her party remains skeptical of an expanded American military presence but supports the agreement because Greenland participated directly in the negotiations.

“Diplomacy proved to be the strongest weapon,” she said.

Flemming Møller Mortensen, speaking for the Social Democrats, praised Denmark and Greenland for establishing shared red lines and maintaining them. He said the agreement strengthens NATO security without compromising the sovereignty of the Kingdom of Denmark.

Jacob Jensen of Venstre emphasized the distinction between granting the United States military access and transferring sovereign authority. He cited a Danish government assessment that the agreement does not give Washington governmental powers over Greenland.

Morten E.G. Brautsch of the Moderates acknowledged the anxiety caused by the dispute but said the United States remained an essential partner.

“Although we have experienced challenges in transatlantic relations recently, the United States remains a crucial ally,” he said.

Lars-Christian Brask of Liberal Alliance described the agreement as an impressive diplomatic achievement that had been far from guaranteed earlier in the year.

“Freedom is always worth fighting for,” he said.

Mette Thiesen of the Danish People’s Party welcomed the deal but said her party would seek clarification of some provisions during committee scrutiny.

Lars Boje Mathiesen of the Citizens’ Party offered a different assessment, accusing Denmark’s political establishment of “collective hysteria” over Trump’s threats. He argued that lawmakers had overlooked the constitutional checks on presidential power in the United States.

Greenland’s representatives raise concerns

Greenlandic representatives in Copenhagen also addressed the agreement, with some emphasizing the importance of protecting the island’s interests.

Naaja Nathanielsen of Inuit Ataqatigiit welcomed the deal while recalling the forced relocation of Greenlanders, secrecy and environmental pollution associated with earlier American military activity.

“Most importantly for Inuit Ataqatigiit, no red lines have been crossed,” she said.

Qarsoq Høegh-Dam of Naleraq questioned whether Greenland’s participation in the negotiations guaranteed genuine equality between the parties. He warned that the agreement’s commitments would mean little without implementation.

“Now comes the great task,” he said.

Denmark’s government defends the agreement

Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen introduced the agreement to Parliament and defended its importance for regional security.

In a written statement to the Folketing, Rasmussen described defense cooperation with the United States as “an indispensable contribution to the security and defence of Greenland and the rest of the NATO area.”

He called the agreement “good for the Kingdom, for NATO and for Europe,” arguing that it would strengthen shared security across the Arctic and North Atlantic.

Rasmussen also said the deal demonstrated the “continued strong ties between Greenland, Denmark and the United States” despite tensions over Trump’s ambitions.

He pointed to “increased military activity by adversaries and the growing strategic interest in the region” as reasons for closer cooperation.

What happens next?

Greenland’s parliament approved the agreement on November 3 by 16 votes to none, with seven abstentions.

Naleraq opposed the deal because it did not guarantee financial payments and called for a referendum.

The Folketing began debating the agreement on November 12, with a final vote scheduled for November 19. If approved, it is expected to enter into force after the United States receives diplomatic notification that the required procedures have been completed.

title: Kathy Ireland Reveals Her Husband Greg Escaped a Burning Boat Amid Explosion
content:
Former swimsuit model Kathy Ireland has revealed her husband, Greg Olsen, narrowly escaped danger after his boat burst into flames due to an engine exploding.

“Engine exploded and a fire quickly melted all navigation equipment and survival raft! My heart is both heavy and full. Heavy because I know the love, sweat and life you poured into this vessel,” Ireland, 63, wrote via Instagram on Sunday, November 15. “Full because of the outpouring of love and support. I’m so thankful God gifted you with a brilliant mind to navigate this disaster so seamlessly.”

Ireland added that Olsen, a former physician who retired to pursue commercial fishing, was “out alone” amid her being “on the road for business.”

Footage accompanying her message showed the boat, named “the 4th Watch,” rocking out at sea as a blazing fire and thick black smoke gushed from atop.

What Happened to Martha Nolan-O’Slatarra? What We Know About Her Death

A subsequent Instagram post shared by Ireland also revealed what her husband found in the aftermath of the incident. “Greg went to the harbor to assess the damage. The boat and all its contents are no more. Besides our commercial fishing licenses, the only thing on the boat that survived is his Bible,” she captioned three photos from Olsen’s return to the scene. “Completely unscorched! My heart is overflowing full!”

The former Sports Illustrated Swimsuit star and Olsen married in August 1988 and share three children — son Erik, 32, and daughters Lily, 27, and Chloe, 23.

Ireland evolved her modelling career into a lifestyle brand, launching clothing lines, operating events spaces and writing children’s books over the years. In February, 2012, she was named by Celebrity New Worth as the richest supermodel in the world. Forbes magazine also reported at the time that she had sold “an astounding $2 billion worth of licensed products” at retail to make her as big as “Martha Stewart.”

Former 'Below Deck' Stars: Where Are They Now?

Us reported in March that Ireland and Olsen were suing their former business managers amid allegations of negligence, theft, intentional representation, constructive fraud and more.

The lawsuit, obtained by Us at the time, stated, “This case is about trust betrayed on a staggering and unconscionable scale. For over 35 years, defendants Jason Winters and Erik Sterling held themselves out to Kathy and Greg, not only as their managers, but as their family. … But in fact, they concealed and misrepresented information from Kathy and Greg to hide their predatory misdeeds.”

Ireland had claimed the defendants were liable for damages “in the tens of millions of dollars, if not exceeding $100 million.”

Former 'Below Deck Mediterranean' Stars: Where Are They Now?

After the lawsuit attracted headlines, kathy ireland Worldwide (kiWW) chair and chief executive Officer Brittany Duncan shared a statement via Linkedin, slamming the suit. “Kathy Ireland may be spiritually broken, but she is not financially ‘broke,’” Duncan wrote at the time. “I have known this woman my entire life. This situation is deeply sad. … What is being done is beneath the dignity of this firm.”

Us reached out to Ireland’s attorney for comment on the LinkedIn post but did not hear back.

title: Sister Wives’ Janelle Was ‘Excommunicated’ From LDS Church While Pregnant
content:
Janelle Brown opened up on Sister Wives about being “excommunicated” from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints after choosing to marry polygamist Kody Brown.

“I was excommunicated from the LDS church right about the time I was either pregnant with Logan or had just had Logan,” Janelle, 57, revealed during the Sunday, November 15, episode of the TLC series. (Janelle and Kody, 57, share six children: Logan, 32, Maddie, 31, Hunter, 29, Gabe, 25, Savanah, 21, and son Garrison, who died in March 2024 at the age of 25.)

She recalled that after marrying Kody in 1993 and becoming his second wife, the LDS church, which she was raised in, shunned her.

“I was, like, 24 and I remember the letter coming to our house,” Janelle shared. “Kody was not involved. It was just me. Yeah, they excommunicated me.”

Sister Wives' Kody Brown Compares Polygamy and 'Plural Monogamy'

The LDS church practices mainstream Mormonism. Kody and his wives initially practiced Mormon fundamentalism, and were specifically part of the Apostolic United Brethren (AUB), before they all slowly distanced themselves from the religion.

Janelle, for her part, revealed on Sunday’s episode that she still has a “spiritual life” but it’s not under a specific umbrella.

“I have a relationship with God. I just don’t have a church I worship with,” she shared. “I’m kind of waiting for some sign that I need to go somewhere or I belong somewhere. I don’t know.”

Sister Wives' Maddie Reacts to Mom Janelle's Spiritual Divorce Plan: 'Why?'

Janelle also noted that during her first marriage to ex-sister wife Meri Brown’s brother, she actually had her husband join the LDS church.

However, once that marriage ended, Janelle remained close with Meri’s family, who were polygamists, and that sparked her own interest in the practice.

“I felt a spiritual calling. I made this decision. It wasn’t because I was — I thought I was less than. I didn’t think it was because I only deserved this,” Janelle told former sister wife and close friend Christine Brown. “I chose it because I felt like it was a calling and it wasn’t anything to do with my perception of what I was worth or what I was entitled to or what I deserved.”

Christine, 54, pointed out, “You found the value in it. I think we were talking about this the other day, that there was value because you were believing in a community.”

Janelle agreed, adding, “I thought that we would have some sort of really great communal family experience or something.”

While all of Kody’s now-ex wives initially bought into the polygamist lifestyle, three of his wives have walked away in recent years.

How Sister Wives' Janelle Brown Found Out Ex Kody Was Leaving the Show

Christine announced her split from Kody in 2021 after more than 25 years of a spiritual marriage. Janelle revealed in December 2022 that she and Kody had been separated for months.

Meri, who was Kody’s first wife, confirmed her split from the patriarch and father of 18 in January 2023.

Kody is still married to his fourth wife, Robyn Brown, and they are living a monogamous relationship.

What Trump said on Truth Social

Trump wrote on Truth Social that the “Radical Democrat Majority in the next Congress” has made blocking and resisting the investment its top agenda. He added that Democrats “want to leave our Warriors weak and unguarded.” He said the American people want those troops “SAFE and STRONG.”

He then wrote that he was calling on Senate leadership that day to move immediately on the 350 Billion Dollar Reconciliation Bill. His post closed with “The time is NOW,” and he wrote that Republicans “must deliver for our Warriors” while Democrats never will. He also said he rebuilt the military in his first term and is doing it “AGAIN, bigger and better than ever before.”

The Hill reported that Trump directed the demand at Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican. In a separate Truth Social post that day, Trump also went after Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer over Schumer’s remarks about tackling corruption. Newsweek said it emailed the White House and Thune’s office for comment.

Hegseth made the same appeal two days earlier

The demand came two days after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth urged Congress to approve at least $350 billion in additional defense funding. He called the money essential to rebuilding military readiness. Hegseth said $350 billion “at a minimum” was needed for a “generational and historic investment” in the department. Hegseth had repeatedly pressed Congress to approve the package in speeches, at events and on social media.

What the money is for

The $350 billion is part of the administration’s $1.5 trillion defense budget request for fiscal 2027. The package includes $47 billion for expanded munitions production and $17 billion for the Golden Dome homeland defense system. The request also includes more than $48 billion for critical minerals. Of the $1.5 trillion total, $1.15 trillion was meant to move through regular appropriations and $350 billion through reconciliation.

Why reconciliation and why the rush

Reconciliation lets the majority pass spending bills by simple majority and bypass the Senate filibuster. Republicans have little time left before Democrats assume the large new majorities they won in the midterms. Once the new Congress convenes, the route closes to Republicans.

Senate Republicans discussed a new reconciliation bill for hours at a meeting before their Tuesday, Nov. 10 leadership election. Several senators said afterward that the conference had effectively agreed to look for a path. Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, the conference chair, described the commitment as doing everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill.

The obstacle is inside the GOP

The House-passed budget blueprint, a required first step for a party-line reconciliation bill, has stalled in the Senate for nearly four months. It provides only $60 billion for the Pentagon. That is roughly $290 billion short of what the White House wants.

Also on Nov. 12, House Speaker Mike Johnson said Senate Democrats had “obstructed everything.” Politico‘s account, as carried by Yahoo News, noted that GOP divisions are what have left the Senate sitting on the budget blueprint.

Thune has questioned whether Republicans can find the 50 Senate votes needed to advance the legislation, since several GOP senators are skeptical of reconciliation. Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul has called the bill “tone-deaf” and vowed to oppose it. Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley has said he cannot imagine why the Senate would do it. Mississippi Sen. Roger Wicker, chairman of the Armed Services Committee, takes the other side. “We need to get reconciliation done,” he has said.

Republican Senators warn of a shutdown risk

Republican senators are warning that Trump’s push could risk a government shutdown in December. One lawmaker quoted by The Hill predicted that whatever goes into reconciliation, Democrats would take out of appropriations. Senate Democrats have already warned Thune that pushing extra Pentagon money through reconciliation would imperil a deal to avoid a shutdown.

A stopgap funding measure expires Dec. 11 and a shutdown follows unless Congress acts. Some Republican appropriators, including Maine Sen. Susan Collins, have floated attaching emergency defense money to a stopgap bill instead. Aides in both parties increasingly expect the full-year funding bills to slip into 2027.

Democrats’ objections

Democrats have opposed both the size of the defense increase and the war in Iran. In July, nearly every Senate Democrat voted against advancing the annual defense policy bill. Rhode Island Sen. Jack Reed said he could not back a bill enabling an Iran war that Congress never authorized. Connecticut Sen. Chris Coons said he doubted the reconciliation package would ever be enacted. Connecticut Rep. Rosa DeLauro said in June that the plan pairs the biggest defense increase in American history with cuts to nondefense spending.

title: Russell Brand Issues Statement, Says He Is 'Not Guilty' Amid Rape Sentence
content:
Russell Brand has issued a statement from prison, claiming that he is “not guilty” after being sentenced to 10 years and six months for rape and sexual assault.

“Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. As you know, I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening,” the comedian, 51, said in a statement shared by his wife, Laura Brand, via his YouTube channel on Sunday, November 15.

Laura, 39, has begun by stating that “Russell has asked me to read something to you today,” before turning to a notebook to recall her husband’s message. The YouTube post served as the first time Laura had publicly addressed Russell’s conviction and prison sentence, which was delivered in London’s Southwark Crown Court on Monday, November 9.

Russell’s message continued, “The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do. I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey. Little as in small, and hey as in, ‘Hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders prison in Europe.’ The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone.”

Russell Brand's Dad Claims His Son Is a Victim After Sentencing

Russell went to trial for four weeks, ultimately found guilty by a jury on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. Russell had repeatedly denied accusations of wrongdoing, and was found not guilty on two other rape charges and an attempted indecent assault charge.

Laura, who shares three children with Russell, concluded on behalf of Russell, “I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me. Let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us. Please support my treasured wife and family. I feel your prayers. Your brother in Christ, Russell.”

After receiving his conviction and sentencing, Russell has since been accused of misconduct by six additional women. London’s Metropolitan Police later confirmed to Us that he remains under investigation for additional rape allegations from two unidentified women.

Russell Brand and Wife Laura Asked for Prayers in Podcast Before Sentencing

A Met spokesperson stated to Us, “The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations. Files have been submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service in relation to both complainants. Detectives remain in close contact with prosecutors as enquiries continue and further investigative work is carried out.”

Elsewhere in the YouTube video, Laura shared support for her husband, adding that she will continue sharing social media videos after discussing the future of them with Russell.

“Obviously, [it] will take some getting used to for me to even sit here and not have my companion and my person with me,” she told fans. “Although Russell is not here now in this moment, the holy spirit is moving and the holy spirit cannot be restrained. I’m speaking to Russell. He’s OK and he’s praying, unsurprisingly. He’s praying and we decided for me to continue.”

If you have experienced sexual assault, call the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 1-800-656-4673 for confidential support.

title: Justin Hartley's 'Tracker' Has Surprise Episode Change After Cast Exits
content:
The latest episode of Justin Hartley‘s hit show Tracker featured a surprise change after multiple cast exits.

During the Sunday, November 15, episode, Colter (Hartley) took a case in Denver, Colorado, which allowed him to reunite with Reenie (Fiona Rene) and Randy (Chris Lee). He also met Mel (Cassady McClincy Zhang) after the actress was promoted to series regular.

The story line was a departure from the usual format, which usually shows Colter on the road solving a variety of cases week to week. He will largely interact with his team over the phone, so showcasing the characters all in one place marks a shakeup for Tracker.

Tracker quickly found success when it premiered in 2024, following fictional survivalist Colter as he helped solve numerous missing persons cases. Viewers were also introduced to his team: handlers Teddi (Robin Weigert) and Velma (Abby McEnany), hacker Bobby (Eric Graise) and attorney Reenie.

Justin Hartley's Rare Comments About 'Tracker' Losing Multiple Cast Members

Weigert’s character was later written off in the season 2 premiere as her wife, Velma, admitted that they needed some distance. Velma then started working with Reenie, and Teddi wasn’t discussed on the show again.

News later broke that Graise and McEnany wouldn’t return for season 3. In their place, Lee returned as Randy and McClincy joined.

“We didn’t ‘replace’ Velma or Bobby. It’s about where I get the most creative juice,” executive producer Elwood Reid told TVLine in September 2025. “What happened with Randy last year was that he popped in these little pieces with Fiona, and I thought, ‘He makes Fiona better. What if they were in the same space every week?’”

Reid further elaborated on the shakeup while speaking to Us, explaining, “The only rule I really have of the show is each week Colter is going to come to a new place and there’s going to be a new case. How he gets those answers and what he uses on the team, that’s all something that’s up for grabs.”

He continued, “Meeting these [local] weird characters is something we’re going to try to do more of as the season goes on. Just Colter coming in and interacting with other characters. That’s fun to see Justin flex those muscles with really good guest cast members.”

'Tracker' EP Defends Multiple Cast Exits, Teases More Possible Changes

More recently, Reid noted that Hartley’s fan-favorite character was only one constant on the show.

“The audience leans in because they’ve seen that character before. But I think they’re still thinking the central DNA of the show is Colter. With this guy, what makes him appealing is he is a mystery to himself,” he told Us in December 2025. “He’s a mystery to the audience. We see him and his off time putting together some pieces of his past.”

He concluded, “I don’t know if we’ll ever put it all together, but he’s going to struggle to continue to do that. That’s just as far as we have thought. The biggest improvement we made this year — in my opinion — was getting people in the same room. Just that connectivity, I do think the audience is enjoying seeing their characters in the same place physically.”

Tracker airs on CBS Sundays at 9 p.m. ET before streaming the next day on Paramount+.

title: Chad Lowe Honors Late Daughter Fiona on What Would've Been Her 14th Birthday
content:
Chad Lowe has marked what would have been the 14th birthday of his late daughter, Fiona.

“With broken hearts we honor and celebrate our beloved Fiona on what would’ve been her 14th birthday. We miss her more than words could ever express. Our love is eternal,” Chad, 58, wrote via Instagram on Sunday, November 15. “Thank you all for your love, support, and prayers.”

The actor also shared a photo of Fiona performing a beautiful jeté leap in the air. Dressed in an ethereal yellow dress and ballet slippers, the late teenager’s hair flowed wildly.

Lowe and his wife, Kim Painter, announced on September 29 that Fiona had died by suicide.

Chad Lowe Holds Celebration for Daughter Fiona After Death at 13: Report

“We are deeply heartbroken by the loss of our beloved Fiona,” Lowe and Painter, 52, wrote in a joint statement, calling Fiona “a loving young girl who was smart, creative and loved to dance.” (Lowe and Painter also share daughters Mabel, 17, and Nixie, 10.)

The couple continued, “She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents. In fact, she was the light of our lives. Her passing is devastating for our entire family and we ask for prayers and privacy at this time. If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health, please reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988.”

Lowe’s father subsequently mourned the loss of his granddaughter in a separate statement.

Medical Examiner Releases New Details on Chad Lowe's Teen Daughter's Death

“Rest in peace sweet Fiona,” Chad’s dad, Chuck Lowe, succinctly captioned an Instagram photo of the late teenager in a pool.

One year earlier, Chad celebrated Fiona’s 13th birthday with a social media tribute.

“Celebrating Fiona officially becoming a teen today!!” Lowe wrote via Instagram in November 2025. “Keep dancing through life FiBear! Love you soooo much!! ❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️.”

The actor had previously been candid about his life as a “girl dad.”

“I’m a girl dad. It’s so interesting because [I’m] always wanting to have my own experiences and not live in the shadow or follow in the footsteps of somebody,” the Pretty Little Liars alum said on the “Still Here” podcast in 2024. “I feel like having daughters is such an incredible privilege.”

Rob Lowe's Family Guide: Meet Wife Sheryl, 2 Sons, Brother Chad Lowe

Chad, the younger brother of Rob Lowe, further noted how raising daughters shifted his mindset.

“I look at the world from really their perspective, and I see the world and a lot of the injustices in the world from their perspective. It’s not all doom and gloom,” Chad said at the time. “Society is changing. I see how we’re really becoming conscious of the role of women. We may, who knows, have the first female president.”

He added, “[We’re] really empowering women and seeing how much women have to offer. I personally think that if women were in charge of nations, we’d be a lot more peaceful.”

If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.

title: ‘Donald, this is on the table’: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed taunts President Donald Trump, demands ‘healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave’
content:
Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed has unveiled a mock gold “TrumpCare” card bearing President Donald Trump‘s signature as part of his latest effort to persuade the president to support Medicare for All.

El-Sayed, a Democrat, shared images of the card on X on November 12, offering Trump the chance to put his name on a universal health care program.

“This is a message for @realDonaldTrump,” El-Sayed wrote. “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

What the TrumpCare card says

El-Sayed shared three images of the mock card, which features the “TrumpCare” name and Trump’s signature.

The back reads: “Show this card at any doctor, hospital clinic, or pharmacy in the United States.”

Its gold design closely resembles the administration’s Trump Gold Card visa program, which offers residency opportunities to wealthy foreign applicants for at least $1 million.

El-Sayed’s proposal is a political pitch rather than an existing government health insurance program. He is using Trump’s branding to make the case for universal coverage.

Why El-Sayed is pushing Medicare for All

The proposal follows El-Sayed’s victory in the November 3 Senate election.

El-Sayed had received 2,520,883 votes, or 52.5 percent, compared with 2,181,108 votes, or 45.5 percent, for Republican Mike Rogers. With an estimated 98 percent of votes counted, AP had called the race for El-Sayed. The figures may have changed since then.

El-Sayed’s political rise follows an unsuccessful 2018 campaign for Michigan governor, when he lost the Democratic primary by double digits.

Eight years later, despite having never held elected office, he defeated Rogers, a former Republican congressman, in the Senate race. He campaigned on single-payer health care, restrictions on outside political spending and criticism of Israel.

In January, El-Sayed will replace retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters and become the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate.

How the TrumpCare idea developed

El-Sayed first floated the idea on November 6 during an interview with Zeteo editor-in-chief Mehdi Hasan. He said he would be comfortable with Trump attaching his name to a universal health care program.

“If he wants to pass Trumpcare-for-All, I’m ok with it. He seems to like to put his name on things,” El-Sayed said.

He repeated the offer during a November 10 appearance on CNN, where anchor Kaitlan Collins asked whether he was serious.

“I’m absolutely serious,” El-Sayed said. “I don’t care what it’s called. I want people to have healthcare in this country.”

He said his preferred system would provide coverage from birth to death without copays, premiums or deductibles, protecting Americans from medical debt.

El-Sayed’s evolving health care proposal

Universal health care has been central to El-Sayed’s political agenda for years.

In a book co-written with Micah Johnson, he described Medicare for All as an expanded version of traditional Medicare that would provide lifelong coverage to every American.

He has also proposed a wealth tax and a governing board modeled on the Federal Reserve. During his Senate campaign, he said workers should be allowed to retain supplemental private insurance provided through employers or unions.

His latest pitch follows comments from Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, who told MS NOW host Chris Hayes that he was “not absolutely certain” Trump would reject a bill lowering the Medicare eligibility age.

Sanders has since urged Democrats to reduce the eligibility age from 65 to 55 as an initial step. He has argued that the proposal could pass the Senate with 51 votes through budget reconciliation.

The Medicare for All Act and its House companion have not received floor votes. The House legislation is sponsored by Representatives Pramila Jayapal of Washington and Debbie Dingell of Michigan. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer have not sponsored the bill.

A separate proposal from Representative Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut would allow Americans to retain private insurance while expanding Medicare access to the broader population.

Trump’s changing position on single-payer health care

Trump has expressed different views on universal health care throughout his political career.

In his 2000 book The America We Deserve, written while he considered a Reform Party presidential campaign, Trump described himself as “a conservative on most issues but a liberal on this one.” He argued that the country needed to “reexamine the single-payer plan.”

In January 2017, shortly before his first inauguration, Trump told The Washington Post that he wanted insurance for everyone but did not support single-payer health care.

By 2018, he had become more openly critical of the proposal. In an October op-ed for USA Today, Trump called the Democratic plan “Medicare for None” and warned it would end the program for seniors.

His rhetoric toward the insurance industry shifted again in November 2025. Trump criticized “BIG, FAT, RICH INSURANCE COMPANIES” on Truth Social and said he would not sign legislation that sent them money.

El-Sayed, who was then campaigning for the Senate, responded: “Just wait until we tell you about Medicare for All.”

Around the same time, Trump told Fox News host Laura Ingraham that a new health care plan would be “so exciting” and that he would “call it ‘Trumpcare.'”

Trump has also promised to become “Mr. Veto” if Democrats won control of Congress, although he has indicated that he remains open to negotiations.

Trump’s health care record

One of the administration’s biggest health care changes came through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed in July 2025.

The Congressional Research Service estimates that the law’s health care provisions will reduce federal spending by about $1.1 trillion over 10 years, primarily through Medicaid changes.

The Congressional Budget Office projects that the provisions will leave 10 million more people uninsured in 2034. The law also introduced work requirements for some Medicaid recipients.

Enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025. El-Sayed’s campaign said the expiration caused about 130,000 Michiganders to lose or drop their health insurance coverage.

Trump introduced the Great Healthcare Plan in January 2026. The proposal would send subsidy money directly to Americans to purchase insurance and codify the administration’s most-favored-nation drug pricing agreements.

The administration also launched TrumpRx.gov in February 2026, offering discounted prescription drugs.

Meanwhile, traditional Medicare patients in six states are subject to the WISeR pilot program, which allows private contractors to use artificial intelligence to review prior authorization requests.

Democrats have pledged to restore the expired ACA subsidies and reverse the Medicaid cuts after taking control of Congress.

Trump’s name on government programs and institutions

Trump has repeatedly attached his name to businesses, products and government initiatives. His administration and its allies have also put his name on the U.S. Institute of Peace, the Kennedy Center and a planned class of Navy battleships.

Other examples include Trump Accounts, the tax-advantaged savings accounts for children created under the 2025 tax law and TrumpRx. The Trump Gold Card and the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, a proposed transit corridor tied to an agreement between Armenia and Azerbaijan, also carry his name.

His image has appeared on other government-related items. The Commission of Fine Arts approved a 24-karat gold commemorative coin featuring his likeness, while the State Department developed limited-edition passports bearing an illustration of the president.

Presidential historian Jeffrey Engel of Southern Methodist University told the Associated Press that the United States had never before consistently named things after a sitting president.

Sanders has introduced legislation that would prohibit naming federal buildings or land after a sitting president.

El-Sayed’s campaign and political criticism

Affordability, corporate influence in politics, Medicare for All and ending funding for foreign wars were central to El-Sayed’s campaign.

During his Detroit victory speech, he addressed Republican attacks on his religion and connected them to economic concerns, saying his name and faith “are not why you can’t afford your gas.”

He also promised to challenge “the corporations and the billionaires.”

“Winning a single U.S. Senate seat was never the goal,” El-Sayed told supporters early on November 4. “The goal is to use that seat to transform our politics.”

During the campaign, he told Newsweek that his priorities included the cost of groceries and housing, access to health care, public schools and U.S. spending on foreign conflicts.

His agenda has also attracted criticism from within the Democratic Party.

During the primary, Michigan state Senator Mallory McMorrow, who also sought the Senate seat, accused El-Sayed of changing his position on private insurance. She urged him to be “honest about what you’re fighting for.”

Some members of Michigan’s Jewish community criticized his comments about Israel. After an attack on a Michigan synagogue in 2026, El-Sayed said “hurt people hurt people,” a remark for which he later apologized. His campaign appearances with streamer Hasan Piker also drew criticism.

Representative Haley Stevens, a Michigan Democrat whom El-Sayed defeated in the August primary, endorsed Rogers on November 1. She said El-Sayed had not adequately addressed the concerns of some communities.

What happens next

Democrats are scheduled to take control of both chambers of Congress on January 3, giving El-Sayed an opportunity to push his health care agenda.

However, most legislation still needs 60 votes to overcome a Senate filibuster. Any bill that reaches Trump’s desk could also face a presidential veto.

Narrower proposals, including restoring ACA subsidies and limiting prior authorization requirements in Medicare Advantage, may have a better chance of becoming law.

The Republican-led House Budget Committee has estimated that Medicare for All would add approximately $47.4 trillion to federal deficits between 2027 and 2036.

El-Sayed’s TrumpCare proposal is therefore an unusual opening offer to a president whose past positions on universal health care have shifted. Whether Trump embraces the idea remains unclear, but the incoming senator has made clear that he is willing to let the president take the credit if it helps deliver coverage for Americans.

title: Rosie O'Donnell Shares 'Creepy' Pic of Figurine of Herself Holding Grandchild

title: ‘We need new leadership’: Top Dem Chuck Schumer gets bad news from within his own party as Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen announces he’s running for Senate majority leader
content:
Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced his bid for Senate majority leader, setting up the first contested race for the top Democratic leadership post in the Senate in decades.

Van Hollen made the announcement during an interview on MS NOW‘s The Briefing with Jen Psaki, one day after Democrats secured control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections.

“It’s now on us to meet this moment and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

The challenge puts Van Hollen directly against New York Sen. Chuck Schumer, who has said he expects to retain his leadership position.

Van Hollen makes his case

Van Hollen said voters in the midterm elections “called for change” and rejected Donald Trump‘s policies as well as “the status quo that isn’t working for working people.”

Van Hollen has served in the Senate since 2017 after spending 14 years in the House. He described the election results as “a generational opportunity” for Democrats to respond to voters’ demand for change.

During his interview with Jen Psaki, Van Hollen was asked what had changed since the previous weekend, when he appeared less interested in pursuing the leadership position.

He pointed to the election results and said voters had delivered a mandate.

Schumer pushes back

Schumer has made clear that he expects to remain Democratic leader.

Before Van Hollen formally entered the race, Schumer told reporters, “I’ll be reelected as majority leader.”

After Van Hollen’s announcement, Schumer said he welcomed a discussion about the future of the Democratic caucus while maintaining that he had enough support to win.

“I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer said in a statement. He added that he looked forward to “leading our new Democratic majority.”

The Associated Press reported that Schumer has said he has the support needed to prevail.

Who is backing Van Hollen

Sen. Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, endorsed Van Hollen on November 12.

“The American people voted for change,” Sanders wrote on X.

Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who has supported Van Hollen for months, also backed him after the announcement.

Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal has said he is open to new leadership if a challenger enters the race.

Schumer’s supporters, meanwhile, have pointed to his role in helping Democrats regain the Senate.

New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, who chaired the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee during the election cycle, said Schumer “understands politics well” and won the Senate back.

Wisconsin Sen. Tammy Baldwin also backed Schumer, using a baseball comparison to argue against changing leadership after a successful election.

“The Brewers just had a record season,” Baldwin said, “and next year is not the time to change our management.”

How the leadership fight began

Democrats won control of Congress in the November 3 midterms, flipping enough Republican-held Senate seats to secure a majority while also gaining seats in the House.

The party needed to flip at least four Republican-held Senate seats to take control and ultimately gained seven.

Schumer has led Senate Democrats while they were in the minority since 2025. He is positioned to become majority leader when the new Congress convenes.

But questions about his leadership had been growing before Election Day.

Progressive activists and some incoming senators encouraged Van Hollen to challenge Schumer. Those calls intensified after Democrats’ strong election performance.

The contest now represents the first serious challenge for the top Democratic Senate leadership position in decades.

What happens next

Senate Democrats are expected to hold a secret-ballot leadership election in early December. CNN reported that the vote is scheduled for December 1.

The winner needs a simple majority of the Democratic caucus, meaning at least 28 votes.

The leadership contest has already drawn Republican criticism.

Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee, wrote on X that the “leadership brawl previews the D.C. Democrats’ agenda: chaos, infighting and a race to see who can sell their soul to the far left fastest.”

The contest between Van Hollen and Schumer will now test whether Democrats believe their midterm victory calls for a change in Senate leadership or whether they want Schumer to guide the party into the new majority.

title: Tom Arnold, 67, Calls People His Age 'Disgusting,' Admits He Hasn't Dated
content:
Tom Arnold is opening up about his dating mindset amid his ongoing hiatus from the romance scene.

“I used to say, people are like — because I haven’t had a date for nine and a half years — ‘You should date someone your own age,’” Arnold, 67, told Page Six in an interview published on Friday, November 13. “And I’m like, ‘Dude, have you seen people my age? We are freaking disgusting.’”

“But here’s the thing,” he continued, “I have learned there’s a lot of funny, smart, sexy, 60-something women. … But I’ll tell you what they’re not looking for. They’re not looking for a guy that used to have a lot of money and now has two little kids. They are like, ‘Forget that. That is not what I’m looking for.’”

Arnold, who confirmed he was serious about wanting to find love again, shared that “it would be good to love somebody and be loved.”

Tom Arnold Says Roseanne Is ‘Not Even Close’ to Being His Craziest Ex-Wife

“I love my kids so much. There’s a lot of love there. And my buddies,” he said. “But I’ll be OK. You know, I’ve had four marriages.”

Arnold was previously married to Roseanne Barr from 1990 to 1994, Julie Armstrong from 1995 to 1999, Shelby Ross from 2002 to 2008 and Ashley Groussman from 2009 to 2020. Arnold and Groussman share two children: son Jax, 13, and daughter Quinn, 10.

In 2025, Arnold got candid about his marriage to Barr while promoting his My Crazy X-Wife comedy tour.

“People say ‘My Crazy X-Wife, oh, I know which one that is. It’s Roseanne,’” he told Us. “And I’m like, ‘She’s not even close to my craziest ex-wife because we didn’t have kids together.’ The worst thing she did was go on Saturday Night Live and say I have a three-inch penis, which is confidential information. You take that to the grave.”

Roseanne Barr Jokingly Wishes Randy Quaid 'Would Leave His Wife' for Her

“Even a 747 looks small when it flies over the Grand Canyon,” he quipped.

The next year, Barr came to her ex’s defense when producer Chuck Lorre — who worked alongside the pair during her show — claimed in his book that the Roseanne writers put Arnold’s name on scripts he didn’t write.

“Unbelievably — I don’t think you’ll hear me say this often — but Tom Arnold is telling the truth for once,” she told The Hollywood Reporter in October. “Talk about the paradigm switch here. Tom Arnold is defending me. I have to thank him for that. That’s the first time he’s done something right by me in his f***ing life. Thanks, Tom.”

Arnold then reacted to Barr’s comments, writing via X, “Don’t give up. Don’t ever give up. 33 years ago I predicted I would do something so cool my 1st X Wife Roseanne would be forced to say something almost nice about me. Hell finally froze over today.”

title: ‘I’d beat him easily’: Donald Trump calls Barack Obama ‘highly overrated,’ says he’d win in a hypothetical matchup because he ‘got many more votes’ than the former president
content:
President Donald Trump said he could “easily” defeat former President Barack Obama in a hypothetical presidential matchup, while calling his predecessor “highly overrated.”

Trump made the comments on November 12, 2026, during a White House interview with Stephen A. Smith, host of the Straight Shooter podcast. He pointed to his vote totals in Texas and Florida as evidence that he could defeat Obama.

The comments came after Republicans suffered major losses in the November 3 midterm elections and as Trump continues to face questions about his political standing and the possibility of a third presidential term.

Trump says he would beat Obama

Smith asked Trump about a hypothetical election between the two presidents.

Trump responded by citing his performance in states with large populations.

“I got many more votes than he got. And I got many more votes in the states… I have most of the state records of the big states. If you take a look at Texas, I have the all-time record, Florida I have the all-time record,” Trump told Smith.

Smith then asked whether Trump was saying he would beat Obama.

“Yeah, I think I’d beat him easily, yeah. I think he’s highly overrated,” Trump said.

Trump continued by criticizing Obama’s presidency.

“I just think, that’s just my opinion, I think he’s overrated. I didn’t think he was a good president, I thought he was a divider.”

Smith then asked Trump how he would describe himself.

Trump said he was “as a person that brings people together” and attributed that ability to “success.”

Smith pressed him on how exactly he brings people together.

Newsweek contacted the office of Barack and Michelle Obama through an online portal on the night of November 12 for comment.

The interview also covered the Iran war, working with Democrats for the remainder of Trump’s term, gasoline prices, immigration and his legacy.

Trump points to vote totals

Trump’s argument relied heavily on raw vote totals.

In the 2024 presidential election, Trump won all the swing states and the popular vote. He received about 77.3 million votes compared with 75 million for Vice President Kamala Harris.

Obama received about 65.9 million votes when he defeated Republican Mitt Romney in the 2012 presidential election.

Trump also pointed to his records in Florida and Texas.

In Florida, Trump received 6,110,125 votes in 2024 compared with Harris’ 4,683,038, according to the Florida Department of State Division of Elections.

Obama received 4,237,756 votes in Florida in 2012, while Romney received 4,163,447.

State voting data reviewed by Newsweek going back more than 40 years showed Trump received more votes than any previous presidential nominee in Florida.

In Texas, Trump received 6,393,597 votes in 2024 compared with Harris’ 4,835,250.

Obama received 3,294,440 votes in Texas in 2012, while Romney received 4,555,799.

Newsweek also reviewed decades of Texas election data and found Trump had received the state’s highest presidential vote total.

However, raw vote totals do not provide a direct comparison between candidates from different election cycles.

Axios reported that population growth has contributed significantly to higher vote totals in recent elections, along with increased turnout.

Texas has long been a Republican stronghold in presidential elections, while Florida has shifted increasingly toward the GOP and is now considered a reliable Republican state.

The third-term question

The exchange was framed by Fox News as a hypothetical third-term matchup.

Trump’s ability to run again is restricted by the 22nd Amendment, which says no person can be elected president more than twice.

Trump won the presidency in 2016 and again in 2024.

He has nevertheless continued to discuss the possibility of another campaign. On November 1, Trump said he would “love to run” again but did not announce a candidacy or explain how he could overcome the constitutional limit.

Robert Collins, a professor of public policy at Dillard University, told Newsweek on November 12 that Trump’s comments were primarily aimed at his political base.

“This is clearly just President Trump throwing red meat to his base,” Collins said. “Given the president currently has a national job approval rating in the 30s, no rational observer believes he could beat Obama in a head-to-head matchup right now.”

Collins also said there was no serious legal path for Trump to seek a third term.

“His past remarks on the possibility of running for a third term are also just trying to keep his base happy. No serious constitutional scholar believes there is any legal way for President Trump to run for a third term,” he said.

Obama has an advantage in polling

Trump’s claim is also at odds with recent polling comparing the two presidents’ public standing.

A CNN-SSRS poll conducted May 7-31 among 2,480 respondents found that 57 percent had a favorable opinion of Obama, compared with 32 percent who viewed him unfavorably.

Trump had a 34 percent favorability rating and a 55 percent unfavorable rating in the same poll.

When respondents were asked which president they admired most, 30 percent chose Obama compared with 19 percent for Trump.

A Pew Research Center survey of 8,512 respondents conducted January 20-26 found that 36 percent said Obama had done the best job among recent presidents, while 13 percent ranked him second best, giving him a combined 49 percent.

Trump received 19 percent as the best-performing president and 12 percent as second best, for a combined 31 percent.

A YouGov/Economist poll of 1,685 U.S. citizens conducted November 9-11 put Trump’s approval rating at 32 percent, compared with 63 percent who disapproved. The poll had a 3 percentage point margin of error.

The comments drew criticism

Trump’s comments prompted ridicule from a CNN panel.

Panelist Rieckhoff joked: “Donald Trump would beat Barack Obama in a Big Mac eating contest.”

Smith has also previously questioned whether Obama would necessarily win such a hypothetical race.

On an episode of The Stephen A. Smith Show, he said he once believed Obama would “smoke him” but had become less certain after Harris’ defeat.

Trump and Smith have clashed before

The interview came after a public falling-out between Trump and Smith.

In an October 30 column, Front Office Sports noted that Trump had previously dismissed Smith as an “arrogant fool.”

Trump had also called Smith “a smart guy” and said he would like to see him run for president.

Trump has used the “highly overrated” characterization of Obama before. Black Enterprise reported that Trump used the phrase in material from journalist Bob Woodward’s book.

Midterm losses shape the backdrop

Trump’s comments came less than two weeks after Republicans suffered major losses in the November 3 midterm elections.

The Senate began the year with a 53-47 Republican majority and NPR reported that few expected Democrats to put the chamber at risk.

As of 3:14 p.m. IST on November 13, Associated Press results showed Democrats with 255 House seats won and Republicans with 169. Eleven seats were listed as won by no party in the AP results, which did not specify why or which party those seats would ultimately favor.

In the Senate, Democrats had 21 seats won and 34 holdovers, for 55 seats including two independents who caucus with Democrats. Republicans had 13 seats won and 31 holdovers, for 44. One seat was listed as won or held by no party.

The AP figures were subject to change as remaining races were finalized and the “Majority reached” and “Control reached” labels were not themselves AP calls.

House Speaker Mike Johnson said Republicans would have needed to defy more than a century of midterm history to retain the House.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer told reporters in Washington, “Relief is on the way.”

The results echoed the 2010 midterms, when Democrats suffered major losses while Obama was president.

Trump and Obama clashed before the election

Trump and Obama held rival rallies in Georgia and Ohio on October 28, just days before the midterm elections.

The two presidents traded criticism over the Iran war, tariffs and the economy.

Obama argued that the war had made Americans less safe, while Trump defended his military campaign and attacked the 2015 Iran nuclear deal negotiated during Obama’s presidency.

Obama also criticized Trump over the cost of living, arguing that the president had focused on projects such as a White House ballroom and a helipad rather than lowering prices.

According to the Daily Beast, Trump responded with a late-night attack on Obama following the former president’s first midterm rally.

Trump’s latest comments therefore revive a long-running political rivalry at a time when his own party is facing a difficult post-midterm environment.

Despite Trump’s confidence that he would beat Obama “easily,” the hypothetical matchup cannot occur under the current constitutional rules and recent polling gives Obama the stronger favorability position.

title: Andrew Shue Breaks Silence After Marilee Fiebig Wedding: 'New Beginning'

Robach and Holmes were axed from ABC in the wake of the scandal. The pair have since given fans a glimpse of their relationship via their podcast and before saying “I do” in a private Arkansas ceremony on September 19, according to a county clerk who spoke to Us in October.

Prior to her marriage to Holmes, Robach was previously married to Tim McIntosh from 1996 to 2008. The pair share daughters Ava and Annalise. She was later married to Shue from 2010 to 2023.

Good Morning America's Amy Robach and T.J. Holmes' Relationship Timeline

Holmes, meanwhile, tied the knot with Amy Ferson in 2004 and the pair welcomed daughter Brianna and son Jaiden. Holmes and Ferson split in 2007. He was married to Fiebig from 2010 to 2023. The exes share a daughter, Sabine.

title: Liberal podcast hosts apologize for laughing at ‘insensitive joke’ about late Charlie Kirk following mass exodus of advertising partners: ‘We should not have laughed’
content:
Jennifer Welch and Angie “Pumps” Sullivan, co-hosts of the progressive podcast I’ve Had It, apologized after laughing at a joke about the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk as a growing list of advertisers cut ties with the show.

The hosts posted their apology on the podcast’s Instagram account, two days after the episode containing the joke was released.

“At least 10 brands have ended advertising relationships, ruled out future placements or distanced themselves from the show.” The companies include Cash App, Boll & Branch, Zenni Optical, Chewy, iRestore, Casper, Nobl Travel, Honeylove, HexClad and Monarch Money.

Hosts apologize for the joke

“On Thursday’s show, we laughed at a joke about Charlie Kirk,” the hosts wrote. “It was an insensitive joke and we should not have laughed. We regret it and we apologize.”

They added that “there is nothing funny about gun violence” and said they had donated to Everytown for Gun Safety.

The hosts also said they have long supported common-sense gun safety reforms and pledged to continue using their platform to advocate for the safety of Americans.

Welch gave a similar explanation.

“We laughed at an insensitive joke. We regret it and we apologized,” she said. “We removed the segment from the episode because we oppose gun violence in all of its forms and made a donation to Everytown for Gun Safety to put our money where our mouth is.”

How the controversy started

The controversy stemmed from the November 5 episode, which featured Welch and Sullivan reading social media reactions to the November 3 midterm elections.

One post read: “We’re digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again.”

Kirk was fatally shot while speaking at Utah Valley University in September 2025.

The hosts laughed as the post was read, with Welch managing to say “No comment.” A clip of the exchange subsequently spread across social media.

The reaction quickly moved beyond online criticism as advertisers began responding to questions about their relationships with the podcast.

Advertisers cut ties

Cash App confirmed it was no longer a sponsor of the podcast. Chewy said it did not sponsor or support the show and “unequivocally” condemned violence.

Honeylove said it had ended its advertising partnership, while Casper said it had ended its sponsorship and would “no longer be associated with that program.”

iRestore said it had “severed all ties” with the podcast and canceled future advertising.

Nobl Travel said it was no longer a sponsor and did not condone “violence or the promotion of violence in any form.”

HexClad said it was no longer advertising with the podcast and had no future placements planned.

Boll & Branch said it did not currently advertise on the show and “will not in the future.”

Monarch Money said its advertising relationship with the podcast had ended in September 2026, meaning it was not a sponsor of the episode at the center of the controversy.

Lists of purported sponsors circulated online, prompting social media users to contact brands and question their connections to the podcast.

Hosts accuse Turning Point USA of driving backlash

Welch and Sullivan also pushed back against Turning Point USA, accusing the conservative organization of “spearheading” an effort to cancel the podcast.

They released an episode on November 9 titled “Not Today, TPUSA,” with the description: “Turning Point wants to cancel us.”

Welch told Newsweek that Turning Point USA was “leading the cancellation against us.”

She accused the organization of mocking violence and refusing to apologize for its own conduct.

“We still have plenty of advertisers and we aren’t going anywhere,” Welch said. “Each and every day we will relentlessly fight for equality and justice for every American and we enthusiastically welcome the nearly 30,000 new followers that have come to our channel in the last few days.”

Newsweek noted that the follower figure had not been independently verified.

In a video posted November 8, Welch called Turning Point a “hateful organization.” Sullivan said she was “not going to be lectured by these people” and told the group to “f— all the way off,” according to Fox News.

Turning Point denies involvement

Turning Point USA denied coordinating an advertiser boycott.

A representative told Newsweek that Welch and Sullivan “have nobody to blame but themselves for the fact that their sponsors are cutting ties.”

The representative added: “It should be no surprise that advertisers don’t want to be associated with their vile hatred and dehumanization of a father and husband.”

Andrew Kolvet, a Turning Point USA spokesperson, wrote on X: “Just don’t legitimize political violence.”

“You can blame me or Turning Point all you want, but we’re not the reason all your sponsors are fleeing. You are,” he added.

Kolvet told Fox News Digital that the organization did not coordinate the boycott and that the backlash developed organically.

Disputed claims and a new sponsor offer

Fox News reported that a source in the office of a prominent nationally elected Democrat called Welch a “sicko.” The source claimed Welch had sought advice about handling the backlash and estimated that the podcast lost “tens of thousands” of dollars in sponsorships over the weekend.

The source also alleged that Welch’s team used ChatGPT to help prepare its response.

Welch denied the claims in a text message to Fox News Digital, saying she had not spoken with a senior Democrat and that the podcast had not used ChatGPT. Fox News did not identify the source.

On November 10, Welch endorsed Minocqua Brewing Company on her podcast after the Wisconsin brewery offered to sponsor the show.

The brewery had previously described Kirk as a “racist jerk” and an “awful human being,” according to Fox News Digital.

Dave Chappelle also faces criticism

The controversy comes as comedian Dave Chappelle faces separate criticism over comments about Kirk’s killing during a Karmageddon stand-up performance at Madison Square Garden in New York.

In footage from his November 7 performance, Chappelle discussed the fear that can come with being a public speaker before turning to Kirk.

“Ever since that guy Charlie Kirk got murdered and I shouldn’t say this publicly, but I feel better,” Chappelle said.

He acknowledged that he knew he “shouldn’t say that” but said he had not asked to feel that way.

“I just be driving around like, ‘Why am I in such a good mood? Oh!’” he joked.

Erika Kirk responded on X without naming Chappelle, Welch or Sullivan.

“To see leftist podcasters, comedians and commentators laugh about political assassination as though it’s entertainment and the destruction of a human life is a punchline, is beyond disgusting,” she wrote.

“You do not have to agree with someone’s politics to recognize the value of their life,” she added.

Kirk said political violence should “never be something this country tolerates, excuses, or celebrates.”

The backlash against I’ve Had It has therefore moved beyond the original clip, with advertisers distancing themselves from the podcast while the hosts and Turning Point USA trade accusations over who is responsible for the fallout.

title: Jackson Olson Reveals How Girlfriend Maggie Sajak Helped Him Survive 'DWTS'
content:
Savannah Bananas second baseman Jackson Olson has one person to thank for his competition run on Dancing With the Stars – his better half, Maggie Sajak.

“I don’t know what I would have done if I did that whole experience alone,” Olson, 29, who competed in season 35 of the hit reality TV series alongside pro Emma Slater, exclusively told Us on Saturday, November 14, while walking the Nickelodeon Kids’ Choice Awards red carpet at Television Studio City in Los Angeles.

“I really don’t,” he continued. “Because every single time I would get done with the show and I would see Maggie in my trailer, I’m like, ‘Oh my gosh, we can debrief. We can go back to normal immediately.’ And I think that if it wasn’t for Maggie, I might have just stayed in bed for that entire season and not been able to be, like, ‘Let’s just talk about something else right now.’”

He added of his girlfriend’s encouragement, “So having her support was literally everything.”

Maggie Sajak Supports Boyfriend Jackson Olson During His 'DWTS' Debut

Olson was sent packing from the ballroom on October 27 after a shocking double-elimination during Horror Movie Night alongside Tyler Cameron and pro Sharna Burgess.

title: ‘I am not running’: President Donald Trump’s former United Nations ambassador Nikki Haley rules out 2028 presidential bid as Republican succession race takes shape
content:
Former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley, who served as U.S. ambassador to the United Nations under President Donald Trump, has ruled out a 2028 presidential campaign as Republicans begin considering who could lead the party after Trump.

Haley made the announcement during a CNBC interview on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, eight days after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections.

“I am not running in 2028, but I will continue to talk about the things that I care about,” Haley said. She added that she would remain involved in policy debates and support candidates, saying she wants “a strong America.”

What Haley said about 2028

During the CNBC interview, Haley criticized Republicans for failing to deliver results when they controlled the White House, Senate and House of Representatives.

She said the party had held all three for two years but voters had not seen the changes they expected. Haley said voters wanted to send a message in the midterms and had succeeded.

She also addressed her political future on the Build or Break podcast, hosted by Daniel Lubetzky and released Tuesday, November 10. Haley said she had not decided whether she might run in 2032 but did not intend to disappear from politics.

“I’ll never say never,” she said.

The Post and Courier reported Wednesday that Haley plans to remain politically active and already has an idea of the types of candidates she wants to support.

Republicans face midterm fallout

Haley’s announcement comes after a major setback for Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections.

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, ending the Republican trifecta in Washington. An Associated Press tally on November 5 showed Democrats with their largest House majority since 2008 and at least 54 Senate seats.

The results have intensified questions about the Republican Party’s direction and who could emerge as its next presidential nominee.

DeSantis and Christie consider their options

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has been among the most outspoken Republicans responding to the election results. In interviews and at a press conference, he described the outcome as a rebuke of Trump and congressional Republicans.

Asked by CNN’s Jake Tapper whether he was considering a presidential campaign, DeSantis said he “hasn’t planned anything.”

Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, meanwhile, indicated that the midterm results had made him more interested in considering another presidential campaign.

Speaking to WGIR’s New Hampshire’s New Radio on November 11, Christie argued that a Republican nominee associated with the Trump administration would struggle in a general election.

He also described DeSantis as a “Trump guy” and questioned the Florida governor’s consistency.

Vance and Rubio remain potential successors

Vice President J.D. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio remain among the most frequently discussed potential successors to Trump.

On October 20, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that it was too early to discuss endorsing a successor, saying the midterm elections needed to come first.

Vance said around the same time that he had not made a decision about running in 2028. Rubio has also avoided discussing the possibility, telling a reporter he would not address the election in any form.

Analysts assess Haley’s exit

Haley’s decision could reshape the early Republican field by removing a candidate who offered an alternative to Trump’s political approach.

Robert Y. Shapiro of Columbia University told Newsweek on November 11 that her exit could benefit Rubio and potentially Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who is not part of the Trump administration.

Grant Reeher of Syracuse University said that Haley’s decision creates room for a more traditional or moderate Republican candidate.

Prediction markets favor Vance

Early prediction-market figures continue to put Vance ahead of other potential Republican candidates.

On November 11, Kalshi gave Vance a 33 percent chance of winning the Republican nomination, while Polymarket placed his odds at 31 percent. Rubio and DeSantis trailed.

Some Republican lawmakers have already expressed support for Rubio.

Rep. Marlin Stutzman of Indiana told Politico that he hopes Rubio runs, while Florida Rep. Mike Haridopolos said he is a strong supporter of the secretary of state.

Haley’s decision removes one potential contender from the 2028 race, but Republicans still face an unsettled succession contest following their midterm losses. Neither Vance nor Rubio has formally announced a campaign.

title: Dove Cameron Details 'Special' Tribute to Late Cameron Boyce on New Song

Dove Cameron paid tribute to her late Descendants costar Cameron Boyce in her new song “Maybe Heaven Is a Jazz Club.”

“I think it became really special, too, when we put Cameron in the second verse ‘cause that wasn’t part of the plan,” Cameron, 30, recalled of the songwriting process on the Friday, November 13, episode of The Zach Sang Show. “ I didn’t have a second verse written, and when it got to that point, I had already started writing about, like, ‘Tired feet are never sore’ and all of these sort of dance things.”

Remembering how Boyce was an ”incredible dancer” during her lyrical session, the pop star soon realized the song would finally be complete with a recording of the late performer’s voice. (Boyce died in 2019 after suffering a seizure in his sleep. He was 20.)

“’Cause I met him at the jazz club / We’re playing for you from above / Yeah, I’ve seen him on the dance floor / Oh, he can’t get enough,” she sings in the chorus. “Tired feet are never sore / Crowd is begging him for more . Angel, you’re the one we’re waiting for / Baby, heaven is a jazz club.”

Late Cameron Boyce's Parents Still Love Hearing Stories of His Kindness

The song ends with Boyce saying, “So, we’ll see you very soon.”

Before including Boyce’s voice in her song, Cameron reached out to his family for permission. (Cameron has remained close to Boyce’s parents, frequently attending his namesake foundation’s gala and inviting them to her wedding to Damiano David.)

“Being able to include him was really special and having his family’s permission to have his voice on there. I played it for everybody,” she said on Friday. “I wanted them to like it, of course, [because[ I wanted them to feel represented and respected. It’s just, like, my dream way to end the whole record. I think it’s such a special song.”

How ‘Descendants: Rise of Red’ Honors Late Franchise Star Cameron Boyce

In addition to honoring Boyce, “Maybe Heaven Is a Jazz Club” also pays tribute to the Liv and Maddie alum’s late father. (Cameron’s dad, Philip, died in 2011 when the actress was 15 years old.)

“The top, it’s a video of my dad from a childhood video on my fourth birthday, where he’s wanting me to sing for the camera,” she explained. “I don’t think I have that much of that, actually, because … we weren’t, like, a show business family, butI thought that was really special because we we had this idea to end the record with that song and then end it with him saying, ‘One last song,’ which I think is really, kind of, magical that we found that audio.”

title: Republicans call for ‘term limits and age limits now’ after concerning video shows Sen. Mitch McConnell’s blank reaction to reporter’s questions about GOP midterm losses
content:
A video showing Senator Mitch McConnell appearing to ignore a reporter’s question about Republicans’ midterm losses has renewed calls from conservative commentators and Republican officials for congressional term and age limits.

The 84-year-old Kentucky Republican is serving the final weeks of a Senate career that began in January 1985 and is scheduled to end in January 2027.

What the video shows

Newsmax reporter Kilmeny Duchardt approached McConnell at the U.S. Capitol on November 6, three days after the midterm elections.

McConnell was being pushed in a wheelchair when Duchardt asked: “Can I get your quick reaction to the midterms? The GOP’s midterms losses. What do you think is going to change?”

McConnell looked toward the camera and then straight ahead without answering. After several seconds, an aide appeared to wave the reporter away.

The footage was posted on X and viewed more than 4 million times. One version was shared by TheBlaze, while several other outlets reported on the encounter.

Republicans call for term limits

The video quickly prompted calls for limits on how long lawmakers can serve.

John Block, a Republican state representative in New Mexico, shared the footage on X and wrote, “Term limits.” Block represents House District 51 in Otero County and has served in the New Mexico Legislature since January 2023. He is not a member of the U.S. House.

Conservative commentator Shawn Farash wrote on X: “Term limits and age limits now.”

The Facebook account for the show hosted by Real America’s Voice personality Steve Gruber also wrote: “We need TERM LIMITS!”

McConnell’s Senate career is nearing its end

McConnell is already set to leave the Senate.

In Kentucky’s November 3 Senate election, Republican Andy Barr defeated Democrat Charles Booker. AP’s count showed Barr with 55.0 percent of the vote to Booker’s 42.9 percent, with about 99 percent of votes counted as of November 11.

Barr will succeed McConnell, who announced that he would not seek another term. McConnell’s current term expires on January 3, 2027.

The midterm elections determined every House seat and roughly one-third of the Senate, making Republican losses a central focus of the question directed at McConnell.

McConnell’s health has drawn scrutiny

The encounter comes after a year in which McConnell’s health and ability to continue serving have received increased attention.

McConnell was hospitalized in June after a fall that briefly left him unconscious. He later said he had also been treated for mild pneumonia and required rehabilitation and physical therapy.

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear criticized Republicans in August over their response to McConnell’s prolonged absence.

McConnell returned to the Senate on September 14 after missing nearly three months.

He stepped down as Senate Republican leader in November 2024 after nearly 18 years in the position, the longest tenure of any party leader in Senate history.

McConnell also appeared to freeze during two separate interactions with reporters in 2023, incidents that drew widespread attention at the time.

Why congressional term limits are difficult to impose

Members of Congress currently face no limit on the number of terms they can serve.

Senators are elected to six-year terms, while House members face reelection every two years. The Constitution sets minimum ages of 30 for senators and 25 for representatives but does not establish a maximum age.

The Supreme Court addressed congressional term limits in U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton in 1995. The Court ruled that states cannot impose additional qualifications on members of Congress beyond those established by the Constitution.

As a result, congressional term limits would require a constitutional amendment rather than a state-by-state law.

The president, by contrast, is limited to two elected terms under the 22nd Amendment, which was ratified in 1951.

Term limits have broad public support

A Marist Institute for Public Opinion and NPR poll conducted April 27-30 found that 83 percent of Americans supported congressional term limits, while 17 percent opposed them.

Support reached 89 percent among Republicans and 78 percent among Democrats.

The poll surveyed 1,322 adults and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.

Republican lawmakers have also introduced proposals to impose limits on congressional service.

In January 2025, Sen. Ted Cruz and Rep. Ralph Norman introduced a term-limits resolution. Norman described the proposal as “basic common sense.”

The resolution stalled in Congress.

The renewed reaction to McConnell’s video reflects a broader debate over age, longevity and accountability in Congress, but changing the rules would require overcoming significant constitutional and political obstacles.
